lessons.title: From reference to loop gain
lessons.physicalIntuition: The divider samples output, the amplifier turns error into a control signal, the modulator converts control into timing, and the plant converts timing into output. Every scaling changes loop gain.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Write T(s) as the signed product GEA(s) Gmod(s) Gplant(s) H(s) for a compatible voltage-mode linearization. For gm amplifiers, convert output current through the compensation impedance before treating it as control voltage.
lessons.modelingConsequence: Expose each transfer function separately and multiply them only with compatible units/signs. Never omit modulator or feedback gain in the total loop plot.
assumptions: single-loop voltage-mode factorization shown; other architectures may differ
lessons.transferQuestion: If the divider gain halves but the amplifier is unchanged, what happens to loop crossover and DC output setpoint?

lessons.title: Type I, II, and III networks
lessons.physicalIntuition: An integrator increases low-frequency correction, zeros add phase/gain where the plant falls, and high-frequency poles limit noise and unmodeled dynamics.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Derive each displayed circuit's impedance ratio or gm-times-impedance transfer function; factor it to locate poles/zeros. Map every R/C to one mathematical term rather than relying on a topology name alone.
lessons.modelingConsequence: The builder generates the transfer function from the selected topology and validates positive finite component values. It does not treat two vendor topologies with the same label as identical.
assumptions: ideal amplifier within its modeled bandwidth unless nonideal poles are added
lessons.transferQuestion: Move a compensation zero below the LC resonance: predict low-frequency gain and phase-margin tradeoffs.

lessons.title: Crossover tuning and measured loop gain
lessons.physicalIntuition: Loop tuning balances disturbance rejection, damping, noise, delay, and uncertainty. Injection perturbs a live closed loop so the return signal can be measured without destroying the operating point.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Choose target shape using complete loop gain, calculate required compensator magnitude/phase, and use Middlebrook's injection conditions to interpret a return ratio. Specify, rather than fabricate, the separate nonlinear load-step validation.
lessons.modelingConsequence: The frequency-domain lab exposes all loop factors and multiple crossings. The lesson and PSpice guide teach injection-point selection; the web lab does not emulate an injection transformer or nonlinear load step. No fixed fs fraction is graded as universally correct.
lessons.transferQuestion: Why can increasing compensator gain improve modeled crossover yet worsen a saturated load transient?
